questions.question: Who is the first real user of this worker pool? The scheduling heuristics and trust model change dramatically depending on this.

options.label: Just you, multiple machines
options.description: You personally, pooling a laptop + desktop + home server. Single-tenant, single trust zone, no cross-user auth needed.

options.label: Small team, shared pool
options.description: 2–10 devs on a team pool idle laptops/desktops. Multi-tenant, per-user cwd allowlists, mTLS matters, humans may want to ack tasks.

options.label: Your own cloud VMs
options.description: You rent/spin up VMs for bursty agent work. Single-tenant but needs a provisioner layer and ephemeral worker lifecycle.

options.label: All three, in that order
options.description: Ship single-user first, extend to team, layer cloud on top later. Protocol should anticipate all three.

questions.question: What's the one thing broken today that a worker pool fixes? (This becomes the acceptance criterion.)

options.label: Laptop is too slow / fan-loud
options.description: Offload agent processes to a beefier always-on machine so the laptop stays cool and responsive.

options.label: Parallelism ceiling on one box
options.description: Scrolls with 20 parallel tasks peg a single machine; want to fan out across several.

options.label: Repo is only on one machine
options.description: The desktop has ~/repos/frontend, the laptop doesn't — want to run agents where the repo already lives without syncing.

options.label: Team-wide: share idle compute
options.description: Differentiator-driven — nobody else does this, so ship it even without a sharp personal pain.

questions.question: Given your first user is just you, should the MVP actually solve the team-pool story — or ship single-tenant and earn the team story later?

options.label: Single-tenant MVP first (Recommended)
options.description: Ship your-machines-only: shared secret auth, no per-user cwd allowlist, no task-ack flow. Keep the protocol shape team-compatible but don't build the team features yet. Fastest to something working.

options.label: Build multi-tenant from day one
options.description: Accept the upfront cost: mTLS, per-worker cwd allowlist, ack-mode, identity. You ship slower but 'team pool' is real the moment you demo it.

options.label: Protocol-only, no grimw yet
options.description: Define the worker protocol and Placement trait, keep LocalPlacement as the only impl. Zero runtime features shipped; unblocks future grimw without committing now.

questions.question: What if you did nothing here and instead invested in making one big local machine work better (concurrency limits, resource pinning, better scheduling on one box)? What do you actually lose?

options.label: I lose the 'repo lives on that machine' case
options.description: The frontend repo is on the desktop, the backend on the laptop. No amount of local optimization fixes wanting to run an agent where its repo already is.

options.label: I lose cross-machine parallelism
options.description: One fast box maxes out at its core count. Multi-box gives real horizontal scaling for scrolls.

options.label: I lose the differentiator pitch
options.description: 'Distributed AI agent pool' is a story no competitor has. Skipping it means competing on features the incumbents already have.

options.label: Honestly — not much, for now
options.description: One big machine + current LocalPlacement covers 90% of what I actually do today. The worker pool is a 'cool demo' more than a felt pain.

questions.question: Which scheduling requirement do you want the MVP scheduler to handle? Each additional one is real complexity.

options.label: Provider availability (claude/codex installed on worker)
options.description: Route by 'this worker has claude-cli installed.' Baseline — you can't skip this one.

options.label: cwd_root match (repo lives on this worker)
options.description: Route tasks whose cwd is under one of the worker's advertised repo roots. Needed if 'repo lives on machine X' is a real use case.

options.label: Load balancing (least in-flight)
options.description: Pick the worker with fewest active tasks. Simple to implement; nice for fan-out.

options.label: Resource tags (gpu, ram, cpu-class)
options.description: Arbitrary string tags on workers, arbitrary requirements on tasks. Flexible but you'll need to design the matcher.

answers.Which scheduling requirement do you want: Provider availability (claude/codex installed on worker), Load balancing (least in-flight)

questions.question: Since you dropped cwd_root matching, how does the daemon know a worker can access a task's cwd?

options.label: All workers see the same paths (Recommended)
options.description: You assume all your machines mount the same shared paths (e.g. Syncthing / NFS / iCloud / dotfiles-synced ~/repos). The daemon trusts cwd resolves everywhere. Zero scheduler complexity; operational burden is yours to keep in sync.

options.label: Worker refuses tasks with unreachable cwd
options.description: Daemon sends the task anyway; worker checks the cwd exists + is a git repo, rejects if not. Daemon retries on another worker. Simple, self-healing, but can thrash if no worker matches.

options.label: Worker advertises a repo list, daemon filters
options.description: Brings back a form of cwd_root matching anyway — you said no, but this is the lowest-surprise option. Reintroduces the scheduler complexity you just rejected.

options.label: Daemon clones the repo on demand
options.description: Task spec includes a git URL + ref; worker clones into a scratch dir before running. Solves portability but adds a whole git-sync protocol and auth story.

questions.question: What's the minimum-viable worker-failure behavior? The existing daemon already handles local process crashes; remote is messier.

options.label: Mark task failed, surface to user (Recommended)
options.description: Worker disappears → in-flight agents transition to Failed with a 'worker_lost' reason. User decides whether to re-summon. Matches existing crash semantics, zero retry complexity.

options.label: Auto-reschedule on another worker
options.description: Daemon picks a new worker and reruns the task. Simple in theory, but agent tasks are rarely idempotent (they make commits, write files) — silent re-runs are dangerous.

options.label: Mark failed + offer one-click resummon
options.description: Fail by default, but emit a CLI/dashboard action that re-summons with the same params. User-controlled retry without building auto-retry.

questions.question: Do scrolls (orchestrated multi-task specs) need to span workers in the MVP, or stay single-worker per scroll?

options.label: Scroll pinned to one worker
options.description: Whole scroll runs on the worker picked at activation time. Simpler state — no cross-worker task deps. Loses the 'fan scroll across team' story.

options.label: Scroll tasks scheduled independently (Recommended)
options.description: Each task inside a scroll placed individually. Maximum parallelism, but task dependencies and shared state (if any) now cross workers. Matches the 'distributed' pitch.

options.label: Defer — keep scrolls local-only for MVP
options.description: Scrolls stay on LocalPlacement; only single `grim summon` tasks use the worker pool. Ships MVP without designing cross-worker scroll semantics.

questions.question: How should a worker register with the daemon? This decides the operational feel.

options.label: Shared-secret + daemon URL in grimw.toml (Recommended)
options.description: Worker config file pins daemon address + bearer token. `grimw start` dials home. No PKI, no cert rotation. Perfect for single-tenant; awkward if you later want team-pool.

options.label: mTLS from day one
options.description: Generate a CA, issue a cert per worker. Overbuilt for single-tenant but zero-rework later. The 'right answer' that slows you down now.

options.label: Daemon discovers workers via mDNS / LAN broadcast
options.description: Cute but fragile — breaks across subnets, VPNs, Tailscale. Every team-sharing system I've seen eventually ripped this out.

answers.Since you dropped cwd_root matching, how: All workers see the same paths (Recommended)
answers.What's the minimum-viable worker-failure: Mark task failed, surface to user (Recommended)

questions.question: What's the *concrete* problem driving the queue? The roadmap lists several motivations — which one is actually biting you (or you most want to demo)?

options.label: Capacity blowup
options.description: `grim summon` (and `inscribe -c N`) can spawn unbounded processes today; need a global ceiling, not just per-scroll.

options.label: Worker pool needs a scheduler
options.description: Now that grimw exists, the daemon should pull work onto workers based on capacity/capabilities — not push synchronously.

options.label: Provider rate limits / backoff
options.description: Provider 429s and transient errors aren't retried with backoff; users hit limits and tasks just fail.

options.label: Budget / quota enforcement
options.description: Need per-cwd / per-tenant / per-hour caps before any of the supervision/budget primitives later in the roadmap make sense.

questions.question: Who is the queue *for* in v1 — what's the user surface area?

options.label: Invisible plumbing
options.description: Existing `summon`/`inscribe` semantics unchanged; queue is internal. No new commands. Users only notice when admission delays a spawn.

options.label: Visible but minimal
options.description: Existing commands still work, plus `grim queue` to inspect pending/running/blocked, and config keys for limits. No priority flags yet.

options.label: First-class with priority
options.description: `summon --priority high`, queue lanes, `grim queue pause/resume`, full admin surface from day one.

questions.question: What's your tolerance for breaking the synchronous `summon` contract?

options.label: Stay synchronous when possible
options.description: If capacity is available, `summon` still returns with PID + Active state like today. Only block/queue when over the ceiling — minimizes user-visible change.

options.label: Always enqueue
options.description: `summon` always returns a Queued agent immediately; scheduler promotes to Active asynchronously. Cleaner model, but every existing test/CLI assumption shifts.

options.label: Not sure — recommend
options.description: Pick the option you'd defend and tell me why.

questions.question: Pushback: do we actually need a *new* queue, or can we extend what's there? `scroll_keeper` already does per-scroll capacity + conflict-aware dispatch. A queue could be a generalization of that loop, not a separate subsystem.

options.label: Generalize scroll_keeper
options.description: Promote scroll_keeper's tick loop into a daemon-wide scheduler that handles all agents (scroll-bound and ad-hoc summons). Single dispatch path.

options.label: Separate queue subsystem
options.description: New `Queue` module independent of scrolls; scroll_keeper feeds into it. Cleaner separation, more code.

options.label: Minimal: global semaphore only
options.description: Skip the queue for now — just add `daemon.max_concurrent_agents` and a tokio semaphore in agent_manager. Defer the rest.

questions.question: Where does queue state live? This decides restart semantics.

options.label: SQLite table, durable
options.description: Add `task_queue` table; queued tasks survive daemon restart. Scheduler queries on startup. Aligns with existing `events` durability.

options.label: In-memory only
options.description: Queued tasks live in a `VecDeque` in the orchestrator; lost on restart. Simpler, but a daemon crash drops pending work — contradicts "daemon-native" thesis.

options.label: Hybrid: in-memory + WAL
options.description: Queue in memory for hot path, append-only writes to events log for replay on restart. More complex than a table for marginal speed.

questions.question: What admission policies are in scope for v1? (multi-select — narrow this aggressively)

options.label: Global concurrency cap
options.description: `daemon.max_concurrent_agents = N`. Hard ceiling across all agents. Cheapest, biggest blast-radius win.

options.label: Per-cwd concurrency cap
options.description: `max_concurrent_per_cwd = N`. Prevents one repo from starving others. Generalizes scroll's conflict logic.

options.label: Per-provider rate limit
options.description: Token bucket per provider (e.g. claude: 10/min). Needed for real Anthropic 429 handling.

options.label: Provider error backoff + retry
options.description: On transient provider error, requeue with exponential backoff up to N attempts. Touches retry/idempotency — separate roadmap item.

questions.question: Priority — in or out for v1? You said "no priority flags yet," but the queue's *internal* ordering still matters.

options.label: FIFO only
options.description: Strict insertion order, no priority field. Simplest. Scrolls and ad-hoc summons interleave by submit time.

options.label: Two implicit lanes
options.description: Internal: ad-hoc `summon` outranks scroll tasks (or vice-versa) by default. No user-visible flag. Easy to flip later.

options.label: Priority field, hidden
options.description: Schema/queue supports priority u8, but no CLI flag. Lets us add `--priority` later without migration.

questions.question: Daemon restart — what should happen to queued and in-flight agents when `grimd` comes back up?

options.label: Reschedule queued, mark active as failed
options.description: Queued tasks stay queued and are picked up. Agents that were Active when daemon died are marked Failed (their child process is gone). Simplest, matches reality.

Synthesis — here's the v1 shape. Does it match what you want?

• **Problem**: `summon` and scroll dispatch both call `executor.start()` synchronously; no daemon-wide capacity awareness, no admission control over the worker pool.
• **Solution**: New `task_queue` SQLite table + scheduler tick loop in the daemon. `summon` enqueues and returns a `Queued` agent immediately; the scheduler promotes to `Summoning`→`Active` when the global cap and a placement check both pass. `scroll_keeper` enqueues instead of calling `manager.summon()` directly.

• **Restart**: queued tasks reschedule; agents that were Active when daemon died are marked Failed.
• **Surface**: `grim queue` (pending list + live capacity + per-worker breakdown). New `Queued` `AgentState`. CLI `summon` returns immediately; users `grim bind` to follow.
